lessons.0.slides.0.description: Understanding how parcel position within a single Grand Cru affects quality
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Burgundy's Greatest Paradox
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Clos de Vougeot is Burgundy's largest Grand Cru (50.59 ha), but also its most inconsistent. Divided among 80+ owners, with a 60-metre altitude difference from upper to lower slope, the variation in soil, aspect, and drainage is enormous. Two bottles labelled 'Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru' can differ in price by 5–10 times.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🏔️ Clos de Vougeot Topographic Profile (North to South)
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 📍 Differences Between the Three Zones
lessons.0.slides.3.points.0: Upper slope (Haut): adjacent to Musigny, more limestone, elegant and refined — the finest
lessons.0.slides.3.points.2: Lower slope (Bas): near the road, more clay, deep soil, heavier style
lessons.0.slides.3.points.3: Altitude: upper slope 270 m → lower slope 240 m (30-metre difference)
lessons.0.slides.3.points.5: Best parcel: Grand Maupertui (centre of upper slope)
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Upper Slope vs Lower Slope Clos de Vougeot
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Why Not Sub-Divide It?
lessons.0.slides.5.content: Many experts believe Clos de Vougeot should be broken into multiple separate Grand Crus, since quality variation is so extreme. But historical reasons (the entire vineyard is enclosed by a single wall) and vested interests make this difficult. The practical solution: know the parcel position of your producer. Top producers often indicate 'Haut' or a parcel name.

lessons.1.slides.0.description: A deep dive into the nine Grand Crus of Gevrey-Chambertin
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Chambertin: Napoleon's Favourite
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Chambertin (13.3 ha) and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze (15.4 ha) are Gevrey's top Grand Crus. By law, Clos de Bèze may be labelled as Chambertin, but not vice versa. Seven further Grand Crus bearing the Chambertin suffix surround them, each with different character and quality. Understanding these distinctions is essential for any Burgundy expert.

lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: 1. Chambertin & Clos de Bèze — the pinnacle; power and elegance in balance
lessons.1.slides.3.points.1: 2. Latricières-Chambertin — the elegant version of Chambertin
lessons.1.slides.3.points.2: 3. Mazis-Chambertin — directly adjacent to Chambertin, powerful
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🏔️ Location and Soils of the Nine Grand Crus (North to South)
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Chambertin vs Latricières-Chambertin
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Charmes: The Value Pick
lessons.1.slides.6.content: Charmes-Chambertin is the largest in the family (31 ha) and also the most accessible. Although considered the most 'gentle' Chambertin, top producers (e.g. Rousseau, Dujac) make outstanding Charmes at only 1/3 to 1/2 the price of Chambertin — an excellent value choice.

lessons.1.slides.7.points.0: Chambertin: black cherry, liquorice, leather, powerful structure
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: Clos de Bèze: more elegant than Chambertin, more prominent floral notes
lessons.1.slides.7.points.2: Latricières: red berries, rose, silky texture
lessons.1.slides.7.points.5: All: share Gevrey's genetic signature of power

lessons.2.slides.0.description: Exploring the only red Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Corton: The Red Exception of the Côte de Beaune
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Corton is the largest Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune (160 ha including red and white), and the only parcel producing both red and white Grand Cru. Located on the Corton hill, it spans three villages (Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix, Pernand-Vergelesses). Because of its size and number of parcels, quality variation is significant.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🧭 Corton Hill Aspects and Microclimate (Clockwise)
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🗺️ Key Parcels of Corton
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: Corton-Charlemagne (white): south-west facing, white marl — the greatest white wine here
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: Le Corton (red): south-east facing, clay mixed with limestone
lessons.2.slides.3.points.2: Les Bressandes (red): the most elegant Corton red
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: Le Clos du Roi (red): the most powerful
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Corton vs Corton-Charlemagne
lessons.2.slides.5.title: The Legend of Charlemagne
lessons.2.slides.5.content: Corton-Charlemagne takes its name from Charlemagne. Legend has it that in his old age, because red wine was staining his white beard, he ordered this parcel replanted with white grapes. The story's truth is debatable, but Corton-Charlemagne is unquestionably one of Burgundy's greatest whites — second only to the Montrachet family.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 👑 Historical Evolution of the Corton-Charlemagne Parcel

lessons.2.slides.7.points.1: Avoid generic labels: plain 'Corton' may come from lesser parcels
lessons.2.slides.7.points.2: Top producer: Bonneau du Martray (the largest Corton-Charlemagne holder)
lessons.2.slides.7.points.3: Prefer whites: Corton-Charlemagne is generally more consistent than Corton red
lessons.2.slides.7.points.4: Price variation: different parcels from the same producer can differ 2–3 times

lessons.3.slides.0.description: A deep understanding of the five Montrachet Grand Crus and their differences
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Le Montrachet: King of White Wine
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Le Montrachet (8 ha) is the world's most expensive, most prestigious white wine. It straddles the villages of Puligny and Chassagne, in a perfect mid-slope position. Thin limestone soils, ideal south-east aspect, and superb drainage create incomparable minerality, depth, and ageing potential. Four further Grand Crus bearing the Montrachet suffix surround it.

lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: 1. Le Montrachet (8 ha) — the undisputed king, perfect balance
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: 2. Chevalier-Montrachet (7.4 ha) — upper slope, the most elegant and refined
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: 3. Bâtard-Montrachet (11.9 ha) — lower slope, the most powerful and full
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: 4. Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet (3.7 ha) — the elegant version of Bâtard
lessons.3.slides.4.points.4: 5. Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet (1.6 ha) — the smallest, exclusive to Chassagne
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Chevalier vs Bâtard-Montrachet
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Leflaive vs Ramonet
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Both estates are top producers in the Montrachet family. Leflaive's style is more elegant with more prominent minerality; Ramonet's is richer and fuller. Both use biodynamics and practise extended lees ageing. Leflaive's Chevalier-Montrachet is considered the finest white wine after Le Montrachet itself.

lessons.3.slides.8.points.1: Chevalier: flint, lemon, tight, very high acidity, ethereal
lessons.3.slides.8.points.2: Bâtard: butter, toasted hazelnut, full, oily, rich

lessons.4.slides.0.title: The Twin Stars of Chambolle
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 16 min
lessons.4.slides.0.description: Comparing the two Grand Crus of Chambolle-Musigny
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Musigny: Burgundy's Most Elegant Red
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Musigny (10.8 ha) is regarded as Burgundy's most elegant and refined red Grand Cru. 70% is owned by Comte de Vogüé; soils are primarily limestone — very thin, with perfect drainage. The wines are silk-smooth, suffused with floral aromas, the ultimate expression of elegance. There is also 0.65 ha planted to Chardonnay (Musigny Blanc) — extraordinarily rare.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🏆 Comte de Vogüé Musigny Quality Evolution
lessons.4.slides.3.title: Musigny vs Bonnes-Mares
lessons.4.slides.4.title: Two Faces of Bonnes-Mares
lessons.4.slides.4.content: Bonnes-Mares straddles Chambolle-Musigny and Morey-Saint-Denis. The Chambolle side (85%) is more elegant; the Morey side (15%) is more powerful. Top producers such as Comte de Vogüé, Roumier, and Dujac hold parcels on both sides, blending them to achieve a perfect balance of power and elegance.

lessons.5.slides.0.title: The Investment Logic of Grand Crus
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 16 min
lessons.5.slides.0.description: Analysing the investment potential of different Grand Crus
lessons.5.slides.1.title: Not Every Grand Cru Is Worth Investing In
lessons.5.slides.1.content: Investment value varies enormously across the 33 Grand Crus. The elite (Romanée-Conti, Montrachet) are already eye-wateringly priced yet still show strong appreciation potential. Mid-tier ones (e.g. lower-slope Corton, Clos de Vougeot) show volatile prices and poor liquidity. The key is finding undervalued Grand Crus with consistent quality.
lessons.5.slides.2.title: 💰 Investment-Grade Grand Crus (by value-for-money)
lessons.5.slides.2.points.0: Best: Vosne-Romanée Grand Crus (except RC) — steady appreciation
lessons.5.slides.2.points.1: Excellent: Chambertin family, Musigny — top quality but expensive
lessons.5.slides.2.points.2: Value: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis — undervalued
lessons.5.slides.2.points.3: Whites: Montrachet family — fast appreciation but more volatile
lessons.5.slides.2.points.4: Avoid: lower-slope Corton, lower-slope Clos de Vougeot — inconsistent quality
lessons.5.slides.2.points.5: Rising star: Chablis Grand Cru — fair prices, improving quality
lessons.5.slides.3.title: Investment Grand Crus vs Drinking Grand Crus
lessons.5.slides.4.title: Auction Data Analysis
lessons.5.slides.4.content: Based on nearly 20 years of auction data, DRC Romanée-Conti averages ~12% annual appreciation, La Tâche ~10%, and Leroy Musigny ~11%. Montrachet whites have appreciated faster (15–20%) but with greater volatility. The Grand Crus of Morey-Saint-Denis are severely undervalued and have considerable appreciation potential.
